Shiloh (Place)
SHY-loh
proper noun (place)
Hebrew Shiloh (H7887), a town in the hill country of Ephraim; the name possibly means "place of rest" or "tranquillity." Distinct from the messianic title "Shiloh" of Genesis 49:10 (see the shiloh-doctrine entry).

📖 Biblical Definition

Shiloh was the town in the hill country of Ephraim where the tabernacle of the LORD was set up after the conquest of Canaan, and which served as Israel's central place of worship for some three hundred years, through the period of the judges until the days of Samuel. After the land was subdued, "the whole congregation of the children of Israel assembled together at Shiloh, and set up the tabernacle of the congregation there" (Josh 18:1); there the remaining tribal allotments were divided by lot before the LORD. Shiloh became the seat of the ark and the worship of Israel through the era of the judges. It was at Shiloh that the barren Hannah prayed for a son and vowed him to the LORD, and there she brought the child Samuel to minister before Eli the priest (1 Sam 1-3). There the boy Samuel heard the voice of the LORD calling in the night. But Shiloh became also a place of judgment: under Eli's wicked sons Hophni and Phinehas, the worship was corrupted, and when Israel presumptuously carried the ark of Shiloh into battle against the Philistines, it was captured, Eli's sons were slain, and Eli died (1 Sam 4). The glory departed ("Ichabod"), and Shiloh's sanctuary was, it seems, destroyed. Centuries later the LORD pointed back to Shiloh's ruin as a solemn warning to those who trusted in the temple at Jerusalem: "Go ye now unto my place which was in Shiloh, where I set my name at the first, and see what I did to it for the wickedness of my people Israel" (Jer 7:12). Shiloh thus stands as a sobering monument: the place where God once set His name can be abandoned to ruin when His people corrupt His worship and presume upon His presence. Privilege without obedience is no security.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The town in Ephraim where the tabernacle stood for some 300 years through the judges (Josh 18:1); where Hannah prayed, Samuel ministered, and the ark was lost under Eli's sons (1 Sam 1-4); later a warning of judgment on presumption (Jer 7:12).

SHILOH (PLACE), proper noun. Hebrew Shiloh (H7887); a town in the hill country of Ephraim.

Where the tabernacle was set up after the conquest (Josh 18:1) and the remaining tribal allotments divided by lot.

Israel's central sanctuary through the period of the judges; where Hannah prayed and Samuel ministered before Eli (1 Sam 1-3).

The ark was carried out from Shiloh and captured by the Philistines; Eli's sons slain, Eli died, the glory departed (1 Sam 4).

Its ruin later cited as a warning against presuming on the temple: "Go ye now unto my place which was in Shiloh" (Jer 7:12). Distinct from the messianic title Shiloh (Gen 49:10).

📖 Key Scripture

Joshua 18:1 — "And the whole congregation of the children of Israel assembled together at Shiloh, and set up the tabernacle of the congregation there. And the land was subdued before them."

1 Samuel 1:24 — "And when she had weaned him, she took him up with her... and brought him unto the house of the LORD in Shiloh: and the child was young."

1 Samuel 4:11 — "And the ark of God was taken; and the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were slain."

Jeremiah 7:12 — "But go ye now unto my place which was in Shiloh, where I set my name at the first, and see what I did to it for the wickedness of my people Israel."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Shiloh the place is corrupted when confused with the messianic title Shiloh of Genesis 49:10, when its ruin is read as mere history rather than the warning Jeremiah makes it, or when the lesson of privilege-without-obedience is missed.

expand to see more

Place-and-title confusion. "Shiloh" in Scripture names two distinct things: the town in Ephraim where the tabernacle stood, and the messianic figure of Jacob's prophecy, "the sceptre shall not depart from Judah... until Shiloh come" (Gen 49:10), understood as a title of the Messiah (see the shiloh-doctrine entry). The two are unrelated in meaning and must not be conflated. This entry concerns the place; the messianic title is treated separately.

Ruin-as-mere-history misreading. The destruction of Shiloh's sanctuary can be read as a sad episode of Israel's early history and nothing more. Jeremiah reads it as a permanent warning: those in his day trusted in the temple at Jerusalem as a guarantee of God's protection regardless of their conduct ("The temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD," Jer 7:4). The LORD points them to Shiloh's ruin: He had set His name there first, and He gave it to destruction for His people's wickedness. The lesson is sobering and permanent: the place where God sets His name is no security to a people who corrupt His worship and presume on His presence. Privilege without obedience invites the judgment that fell on Shiloh.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The town in Ephraim where the tabernacle stood through the judges (Josh 18:1); where Hannah prayed and Samuel ministered (1 Sam 1-3); the ark lost under Eli's sons (1 Sam 4); its ruin a warning against presumption (Jer 7:12).

The tabernacle set up there after the conquest (Josh 18:1); Israel's central sanctuary for ~300 years

Where Hannah prayed, Samuel ministered before Eli, and the LORD called the boy in the night (1 Sam 1-3)

Usage

"Shiloh — the town where the tabernacle stood through the judges, where Hannah prayed and Samuel ministered."

"The ark was carried from Shiloh and lost; the glory departed under Eli's wicked sons (1 Sam 4)."

"Go ye now unto my place which was in Shiloh, and see what I did to it (Jer 7:12): privilege without obedience is no security."
